title: What does your AI game dev pipeline look like these days?
author: EngineeringAntique50
selftext:
**Hey everyone! 👋**

**I’m just getting started with AI game dev and I’d love to hear how you all approach it. I'm trying to find my footing and get a clear picture of what a typical setup looks like these days.**

**Are you mostly relying on APIs from the big models (like GPT or Claude), or do you prefer running something smaller locally on your own rig? And by the way, does anyone here use Gemini in their game dev workflow😂 Which specific models are you using, and how do they hold up in practice compared to the competition?**

**Honestly, I’m curious about your entire pipeline from generating NPC dialogue, to visuals and audio, all the way to how you actually hook it into your engine. Which tools can you not live without, and what are the main pitfalls to watch out for as a beginner?**

comments.author: Brewgazer
comments.body: There’s info out there on what all you can do but spreading that info is something people don’t do because while these companies are racing for the best ai model, ai game devs are racing to put out the first game on steam that no one can tell used ai for it. What you’ll want to do is pick the company to go with, I choose cursor, then find the skills you’ll need with it, blender, godot, game dev skills. Find the mcps needed for blender and godot or make them. Every game start with having your agent setup md files(don’t know what that is? Go look it up) you can also feed decomps to your model to give it a better understanding of the games your pulling influences from

comments.author: 3tt07kjt
comments.body:
> Are you mostly relying on APIs from the big models…

We use the APIs at work (not gamedev), but instead I rely on the “subscription” which is a lot cheaper.

Smaller / local stuff in my experience isn’t nearly as good so I don’t bother with it. Someone will come into this thread and argue with me about it, probably, but that’s my experience.

> Honestly, I’m curious about your entire pipeline from generating NPC dialogue, to visuals and audio, all the way to how you actually hook it into your engine.

For dialog, visuals, and audio I’m not using AI, except for a few minor visuals like buttons / logos and things like that.

comments.author: Square-Yam-3772
comments.body:
if you are new, pay attention to one-prompt game posts. they usually tell you about their setup and what they prompt

set that up and use the same prompt. once you get a playable game. That's your "hello world"

after that, just explore ways to make better games but at least you have the bare minimum working setup

comments.author: laser_george
comments.body:
Hi, gamedev via AI is the way to go, so congrats on starting this journey.

My pipeline is evolving all the time, new models and tools tend to revolutionize certain steps. I am a hobbyst gamedev, so I need to look at the costs.  
Today I would do all the things with Opus 5.5, but this may change completely when a better offer comes from other ai model factory, and recently it is happening on a weekly basis :D

comments.author: AfternoonMany8117
comments.body:
Definitely use Obsidian MCP and use it as a repo memory, and on top of that, build a handover system. The moment the context starts filling up, hand it off to the next conversation. Input and output tokens will run high, but trust me, it’s worth it. A subscription is insanely cheap compared to the API right now; pick a subscription that fits your budget.

Always build small tools for things like exporting assets or doing minor tinkering.

Use GIT. Use GIT. Use GIT.

replies.author: FinsAssociate
replies.body:
"Always build small tools for things like exporting assets or doing minor tinkering"

could you elaborate on this please?

replies.author: AfternoonMany8117
replies.body:
For example, if I'm going to use a physics library in my project, the first thing I do is spin up a separate HTML file where I can do some tinkering with it. When I tell Claude, "move this card from here at this speed and let it drop to the floor," it might make it too fast or too slow—which happens often, is inaccurate, and costs tokens and time. Whereas if I dial in the speed myself in that tool and tell Claude "do it like this," I get much easier and more precise results.

Of course, I don't build this tool just to dial in card push speed; I reuse the same tool over and over across overlapping areas in the same project. And whenever possible, I always start with HTML because the iteration is so much faster.

replies.author: FinsAssociate
replies.body: Cool, i see. I use html docs for lots of things, but I haven't really used them as tools like that. How do you actually dial in the speed yourself? Is claude able to make an html file that tracks your mouse movement or something?

replies.author: AfternoonMany8117
replies.body: No, but it can read the simulation logs, or since I already want all the numbers displayed on screen anyway, I can just feed those numbers to Claude.

replies.author: FinsAssociate
replies.body: are these numbers that are displayed by the html doc or some other way? (dev console or something?)

replies.author: AfternoonMany8117
replies.body: Exactly, in the dev console depending on how the tool is structured—tailored to whatever numbers I want to see.

replies.author: delusion54
replies.body:
interesting stuff.   
1. I am using obsidian but i manually tell it to update it everytime as a structured wiki. what does the mcp really offer for obsidian?  
2. About the handover, do you ask detailed summaries as md? Isnt autocompacting actually achieve a similar goal?  
3. When you say build tools, do you imply custom skills?

replies.author: muikrad
replies.body:
For tools he probably means small scripts.

For me handover didn't yield nice results. I prefer asking Claude to maintain specs. It's the same thing but more detailed, and it's not aimed at "passing on the work to the next agent", rather it describes the game as it stands.

As for your first question, custom skills are useful, but a good claude.md works too. In that file you can tell it to keep the updated and you won't have to manually ask it everytime.

On my end I use background agents. Then my claude.md file explains that it must go through the scout and planner first, then write tests, then write code. I ask it to decide between a coder or senior coder (coder is opus medium, senior is xhigh) depending on the task complexity. Then it uses the scribe agent to update the specs.

I write todos in github issues and just start my sessions with "go tackle issue #32" and everything else is automatic.

replies.author: AfternoonMany8117
replies.body:
1. Yes, you have to update it manually—at least as far as I know. Even though MCP doesn't offer a massive advantage, it works much more smoothly inside Obsidian and creates the canvases and mind maps you want more effectively. Or it can help while I'm already structuring the project on an Obsidian canvas.  
  
2. With autocompacting, it's way too easy to lose details. So yes, I have it make additions and edits to a dedicated handover .md file within the project. At this stage, you need to establish strict and practical rules for the handover process.  
  
3. No, by "tools" I mean this: for example, I'm using pixel art in my project and generating it with AI as well, so I build small tools for batch cropping, edge cleanups, etc., or a tool for procedural item generation if the project needs items. Similarly, a UI tool to easily feed in-project rules (physics, interactions, connections) into Claude.   
  
Also, I forgot to mention the thing that helps me the most: structured outputs. I ask it to number the sentences in its responses, and if it asks questions or gives options, to format them this way. The output ends up with line numbers like this, so instead of typing everything out, I can simply reply with the numbers:   
  
"1. Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.  
2. Ut enim ad minim veniam, quis nostrud exercitation ullamco laboris nisi ut aliquip ex ea commodo consequat.  
3. Duis aute irure dolor in reprehenderit   
3.1 voluptate velit esse cillum   
3.2 dolore eu fugiat nulla pariatur.   
4. Excepteur sint occaecat cupidatat non proident;   
4.1 sunt in culpa qui officia deserunt mollit anim id est laborum."  
  
 ...like that. Then I just type numbers like 1, 3.1.

comments.author: SteveLittleFish
comments.body:
I type "claude" in my terminal, and then tell it what to do!

In general there isn't much of a "pipeline".  When I'm initially coming up with the spec, I will tell it "I'm going to brain dump, don't do anything until I say go." and I will just deliver a stream of consciousness unto my agent.

At some point I will go over my general guidelines.  Things like "use godot, it will be on the path", "use the blender 4.x install in \~/opt over the cli for models".  Sometimes I drop in a markdown file with my ComfyUI server details if I need gen ai textures or sprites.

Then I tell it to create a CLAUDE.md.  Tell it to commit to main, no branches, push every time it commits.  Never rewrite history, do follow up commits to fix things etc.

I will tell it to enable git lfs if there are assets.

Then before we are done I will make it add a [README.md](http://README.md), and a [TODO.md](http://TODO.md) with a checklist of things to do.

Then, whenever I open a session I either ask for a feature "let's get the transition between ground types looking better..." or I just say "What's next?".

I don't really understand all of these fancy "piplines" and don't see the need for endless MCP servers and skills.  There may be some things I'm missing out on not using the Blender MCP but it seems to do about as good as anyone else's project with just the CLI.

comments.author: Typical_Clock_5286
comments.body:
Right now VSCode with the Codex/Claude extensions. Gets the job done and is more than good enough.

On one particularly difficult task, Claude took it upon itself to create its own MCP to get more control over the unity editor lol.

Has been working like a dream and playing them against each other is great for auditing the state of the project and stopping either one from too much tunnel vision.

comments.author: matthewjosephtaylor
comments.body:
My current approach is to have the AI create a clone of a game I'm interested in making/extending and then working forward from there. LLMs \*love\* clear goals and having a working example to refer to is excellent. From there the world is your oyster and playtesting and providing guidence/feedback is the key. Great artists steal.

The harness/models are in too rapid a state of change to give any meaningful advice other than to not get too attached to anything and always keep your context local and easily searchable (thread history/research notes/code/etc). That context is \*gold\* and all the providers want you to keep it with them, bank that gold wisely.

I'd focus on making the game \*you\* want to play right now, and not be concerned about finding an audience for it other than yourself. IMHO bespoke personalized games are going to be the future of gamedev. Losing interest in the game is the only real danger to focus on.

I'd also say that creating your own pipelines for art and such are part of the fun. Don't sleep on ComfyUI via api and blender api for visuals/sounds/art/etc. Put your AI pal in a room full of easy to use tools and focus on getting them better and better tools to use.  
  
The main pitfall is creating overly complex unmaintainable code, same as always. Focus on simple and fast turnaround.  Good luck!
